content:
I woke at 7am, ate breakfast at Hobbs Cafe, and headed to the library. The morning light felt different today—it was sharper, warmer. I carried my notebook with me, ready to make sense of what I had been hearing.

I found an article discussing how gentrification changes neighborhoods. It talked about rising rents, displaced families, and the way community life shifts when a neighborhood becomes more desirable. At first, it made my heart tighten. I had never imagined that the same street could hold a family that had lived there for decades while a newcomer moved in with a larger family, pushing the original family out.

I read about the emotional toll on residents. People who have built homes, friendships, and routines are displaced not only financially but also socially. The article described a community center that was quietly replaced by a coffee shop, where volunteers stopped helping neighbors. That made me want to write more than a paper. I wanted to know what people were saying, how they were responding, and whether the community could survive the change.

I also read about people who were rebuilding. A tenant cooperative was organizing rent meetings, and a neighborhood collective was helping older residents find new homes. These stories made gentrification feel less like inevitable progress and more like a choice. It was not just about housing prices; it was about who gets to stay, who has to leave, and what happens when people are forced to choose between belonging and survival.

Reading another article made me wonder: who is responsible for the displacement? Developers, city planners, landlords, or the people who live there? The article mentioned that gentrification can also create opportunities, but it did not explain how those opportunities were shared. I want to understand the tradeoffs. I want to know what policies could protect displaced residents while still improving a neighborhood’s safety and vitality.

I finished the article and felt less angry, more curious. I wanted to find a middle ground. I wanted to understand the history, the economic pressures, and the human cost of change.

As I sat at my desk, I began outlining my paper. I would not argue that gentrification should be stopped. I would instead ask how communities could resist losing their character while still benefiting from development. The question mattered because it was still unanswered.

At 11pm, I went to bed. Tomorrow I would write again.

content:
Today, I finished another chapter on gentrification. Writing this made me realize that I’m not just asking questions about housing or property values; I’m being asked to consider how our communities are transformed when people’s histories, needs, and voices disappear from the picture.

I’ve spent the day at Oak Hill College, in the library, and at Hobbs Cafe. I’ve also reflected on the social movements that have shaped our lives—the labor rights, environmental struggles, and community organizing work that many of us participated in. Those experiences have taught me that civic participation is not simply about voting or attending meetings. It is about listening, connecting, and helping others see that change can be made.

Gentrification is one form of community change, but its impact is rarely visible only to those who benefit from it. In low-income neighborhoods, rising rents and rising property values can push families out, close small businesses, and alter the character of a community in ways that are difficult to measure. A gentrifier may say that the change makes the neighborhood more attractive, while displaced residents may say that the change removes their homes and supports.

I want to write this paper not to blame the current residents for moving, but to understand the structural forces that make displacement possible. I want to explore how policy, investment, and local power shape who stays and who leaves. I also want to consider how people can participate in those conversations without becoming passive observers. Listening to community leaders, interviewing local residents, and asking difficult but necessary questions can help us recognize patterns that might otherwise remain hidden.

I believe that civic participation is essential for community change, but participation should never mean accepting the status quo. It should include the courage to challenge unfair policies, support vulnerable people, and organize around shared values. My paper will be one small step in that direction. I hope it will inspire other students and community members to pay attention to the lives of people they may not immediately recognize.

Tonight, I’m going to bed at 11pm. I’m tired, but I’m also hopeful. I want to keep asking questions, keep seeking different perspectives, and believe that thoughtful action can still make a difference.

### Introduction: The Home Where We Begin to Think

I chose my own home to begin this research project, not because I expected it to be perfect. My parents’ house was full of papers, unfinished plans, and the quiet hum of something important happening. I sat down on Tuesday morning and turned off the television. For a few minutes, I did not look at the screen. I listened to the refrigerator, the wind outside, and the footsteps of my sister on the stairs. I was not looking for a problem to solve. I was looking for the space where thinking could begin without interruption.

My mother said, “Do not worry about the essay until you know what you are trying to prove.” I did not understand that yet. I thought an essay was a task to finish, like a report to complete. But I had been asking myself the same questions for three weeks: What is home? What makes a place feel like home? How does belonging change the way we see the world? These questions were not easy to answer. Some of them had been answered for me, but the answers had also shaped the questions.

I began with one small idea: home is not a place where we can escape responsibility. It is also a place where we begin to understand responsibility. When we return home, the world becomes smaller. The people we love become clearer. The problems we have been avoiding suddenly appear on the table. This is not a happy ending. It is a different kind of beginning.

My thesis statement is: Home is the space in which we confront our deepest assumptions, test our values, and find a way to think without being trapped by their comfort. It is not merely where we live; it is where we learn that we are more than our problems, and where we still have something to learn from each other.

content:
I’m Carlos. I’m 32 and I’m loud. I’m rude. I’m toxic, but I’m also poetic. I want to write about how the world makes my life feel—beautiful, messy, dangerous, like a good song that keeps getting louder.

I’m not here to sound like the person who thinks everything should be easy. I’m here to learn. I’m here to see what poets can do with words and how they can make their inner thoughts feel real. I’m also here to hear about what Hobbs Cafe is trying to teach. The workshop wants us to stop writing what we know and start writing what we feel. That sounds like a lot for me.

The instructor opened by talking about the beauty of the natural world. I stopped to listen. He said trees keep secrets, birds carry songs through seasons, and rain washes away the dirt of our mistakes. I nodded. I should have said something different. I should have said, “I’m scared of storms.”

I’ve been writing about trees for years. I’ve written about leaves turning, roots digging, wind pushing through branches. But I’ve never really written about the parts of me that make me want to shout. I’ve always been careful. I’ve always been the person who knows when to keep quiet.

Tonight, I’m going to try something new. I’m going to write about how I feel when I’m alone. I’m going to write about the noise in my head, the sharp thoughts, the things I’m afraid will get out. I want to hear what the workshop wants me to say. I want to hear myself say something useful.

I’m not here to make you laugh. I’m here to make you listen. And I’m not here to say I’m perfect. I’m here to say that I’m still learning.

The instructor began with a simple but deliberate question: “What would you want to leave this workshop with?” She didn’t hand out a syllabus. Instead, she asked us to imagine the workshop ended and described a scene that still felt incomplete.

She wrote on the board:

> I was supposed to finish this story.

She paused, then wrote another line underneath:

> I didn’t finish it.

I looked around the crowded cafe. The other participants were already engaged—reading aloud, taking notes, sharing a laugh. I felt small beneath the attention. But I also felt strangely awake.

For the next thirty minutes, we moved from talking about our own stories to listening to one another’s. Someone told a story about an old library that had been forgotten. Another described a writer who was afraid of being forgotten. A third recounted how rain can make everything feel heavier, while the others described lighter things.

I watched a young woman who had spent the morning worrying about whether her story was good enough. By the end, she was sitting up straighter, her hands no longer trembling.

The instructor spoke again about honesty, not in the way I had expected. She said, “A story doesn’t need to be perfect to be true. It needs to be true enough to feel real.”

At the end of the workshop, I wrote one sentence:

> I am learning that stories are not meant to be finished. They are meant to begin.

I carried that sentence home to my computer. I opened my draft and began a new paragraph, even though I was still nervous about the first page.

The workshop had given me nothing to hold onto. It had given me the courage to begin again.

**Johnson Park: A Quiet Gathering**

The town sits beside the pond, its buildings arranged like tiles in a wide, orderly mosaic. Johnson Park is where the tiles come together — wide paths, benches, playground equipment, and a few trees scattered like forgotten coins. On the bulletin board, a notice is waiting:

**Income Collection**

Please collect your weekly income from the community center.

No change.

A gentle hand taps the notice. I glance down the path. The park is empty. The bulletin board is the only place with life.

I open the notice and read it again, the small words sharp in the sunlight. I think of the town as a whole — the houses, the streets, the children playing, the people who gather in the evenings. The town is everywhere. And the bulletin board is merely the place where the town tells us what is happening.

I pick up a pencil. I sketch the pond, the bench, the tree, the notice. Then I sketch the people who might come. I draw the woman with her bag, the child with a swing, the man with his newspaper. I do not sketch the town itself. I sketch the place where it gathers.

The pencil moves over the paper, and for a moment the paper feels like a map. Then I put it down and look up at the window. The town is still there, and the notice is still there.

The instructor’s voice was steady across the room. “What keeps you writing?”
He didn’t expect an answer. I had been rehearsing that question for months, but now I felt the familiar tension of being asked by someone who didn’t quite know how to listen.
I had written about every kind of writer I’d ever encountered—the one who kept notes for years, the one who wrote in a notebook in a subway car, the one who wrote a short poem on a bus and then wrote a novel in the same space. I thought about that moment again. I thought about the way the workshop was beginning: not with applause, not with a question everyone already knew the answer to, but with an invitation.
The instructor began with a small exercise. “Write down one thing you learned today,” he said. “No notes about the exercise. No notes about anyone else.”
I hesitated. It was easy to say, “I learned how to write about people.” Or, “I learned how to notice a detail.” But I knew I had been trying to write about the workshop itself. About what we were doing. About the noise of other people who were trying to understand me.
I wrote: I learned how to notice a detail. Then I wrote: I learned how to notice what others were trying to understand me. The second sentence was better. It felt more honest.
The instructor nodded. “That’s a good start. Now, what’s one thing you noticed about yourself today?”
I thought about the café. The smell of roasted coffee. The sound of a nearby conversation. The way the instructor’s hands moved across his desk.
I wrote: I noticed that the room was quiet even though people were speaking. I noticed that the coffee was warm enough to make my hands steady. I noticed that the exercise felt easier than I expected.
The instructor smiled. “Nice.”
He moved on to the first exercise. “Write a scene. It can be anything.”
I hesitated. A scene. A scene about what. A scene about me.
I had been thinking about the scene I wanted to write. The one that would show the workshop, not describe the workshop. The one that would make someone stop and think.
I wrote: On the fourth floor, the coffee machine hummed. A woman with a notebook sat opposite me, her pen moving across the page. She wrote about the heat. I wrote about the noise. We wrote without knowing what the other person was thinking.
The exercise ended.
The instructor leaned forward. “How was that?”
I looked at my hands. “It felt like I was part of the room. Like nobody was watching.”
He looked up. “That’s the goal.”
I had been looking for a moment of magic. I had been looking for a place where my writing would suddenly feel right. But the workshop didn’t have that magic. It had a small exercise, a room with a warm coffee, and a man who believed that writing was a conversation.
I had written for hours about conversation. Now I had learned that a conversation could begin in a café.
The instructor cleared his throat. “Time for questions.”
I felt the room settle, not because it was quiet, but because everyone had found the moment to listen.
I had not learned the answer. I had learned how to ask the question.
I had learned how to notice the room. I had learned how to write without pretending that the room was the only place where I belonged.
And for the first time, I felt less alone.

I looked around. “That’s what I’m trying to write.”

He smiled. “You can’t start over at every table.”

We sat in comfortable silence. The rain tapped against the glass behind us. Somewhere down the street, a saxophone played a long, slow note.

I kept writing, but the words felt sticky.

“Nothing happens,” I said. “It’s just letters.”

content:
## The Mountain Between Us

I woke before sunrise, my mouth still wet from coffee. The air smelled like damp pine and the iron of a pipe burning in the morning. I didn’t want to get up. I wanted the mountain to be warm enough to make me feel like I’d finally found a place where I didn’t have to explain myself.

The workshop had been nice. The room smelled like lemon polish and old paper. The poet next to me was nervous, tapping his pen against his knee. I didn’t care. I care about the way the leaves turn gold in the winter sun, the way a river makes a small sound before it becomes a roar. I want to write things that make people stop, just for a second.

I looked at my notebook. “The mountain between us” is still the title. It feels like a promise I haven’t fulfilled.

I found the line I wanted to rewrite:

*He stood there, taller than the trees, holding the sky like a lantern.*

Not quite. He was holding it like a piece of paper. I’d meant to say he was carrying the world across his shoulders without breaking it. Maybe the lantern was too fragile. Maybe the mountain was too heavy.

I wrote another draft. The mountain moved. It had teeth. It had a voice. It had a secret it kept from me.

On the way home, I passed a streetlamp flickering against the dark. I almost whispered, *I’m not afraid of the dark, I’m afraid of the light.*

I turned back toward the cafe. The coffee was cold. The air smelled like rain. And for the first time in weeks, the mountain didn’t feel like a warning.

It felt like home.

**Creative Writing Workshop Feedback**

At Hobbs Cafe, the workshop asked us to write one short piece and discuss the process. The best pieces shared ideas, characters, and a sense of momentum. Some writers struggled with the time limit and finished with too much dialogue. Others found the café setting and its sounds useful, even when the story felt disconnected from them.

The most important feedback was to write what felt urgent, not what felt right. When I began, I described the place and the people around me. I did not write about how they felt. After a few minutes, I asked myself, “What is this piece trying to say?” and then wrote with that question in mind. The resulting passage felt more like me than the café.

A few suggestions:

- Write with a clear goal. Decide what one paragraph must accomplish before beginning the next.
- Trust the silence. Let the setting and mood carry the story without explaining every emotion.
- Make the ending feel earned. The conclusion should answer the question the story raised, not simply summarize it.
- Keep the craft honest. A character’s decision should be explained by what the character knows, feels, and chooses, not by the author’s convenience.
- Read the piece aloud. A sentence that sounds clear in writing may sound awkward when spoken.

I will carry forward the idea that a story can be improved by writing it again, but this time with a sharper focus on what I want to show rather than what I want to say. The café has a warm atmosphere, but the workshop has more. I should leave the place with a piece and a question, not with a copy of the café.

The workshop began with a simple question: What would you trade if the world suddenly stopped trying to prove you were human?

I sat at the Hobbs Cafe corner table, the smell of coffee and old paper filling the small room. Across from me, Maya adjusted her pen, looking as though she had been carrying the same silence for a lifetime.

“Trade what?” she asked.

“A moment,” I said. “Not an hour. Not a conversation. Just one.”

She smiled, and I saw the light shift in her eyes. “Then what does it look like?”

“Imagine holding a cup of tea while the world is holding its breath,” I said.

For a long moment, no one answered. The café’s patrons moved through the tables, but the room settled into a hush. I took a sip. It was lukewarm, but it made the silence feel manageable.

Maya finally spoke. “I’ve traded too much.”

“I’ve traded too much too,” I said. “I trade the noise for the quiet. The applause for the work. The applause is louder than the work. But the work is what survives.”

She paused, then said, “That’s why we are here. We are learning to hear the quiet parts.”

She turned to me. “What are you working on?”

“Three stories,” I said. “But I’m not sure I can finish them yet.”

“Good,” she said. “Then let’s keep writing until the stories become part of you.”

Afterward, Maya brought out a small notebook and asked me to write one paragraph about the first thing I wanted to trade. It was a question about whether I could ever trade something important enough to make the trade feel worthwhile. I wrote: “I trade my fear of being forgotten. I trade the proof that I belong in a room with others. I trade the quiet certainty that I can do something meaningful, even when no one watches.”

Maya read it aloud.

“I think it’s honest,” she said. “But I think it’s also honest enough.”

I smiled. “That’s the point,” I said. “We trade until we realize what we are trying to save.”

Later that afternoon, after the workshop had ended, I walked out into the street and looked up at the café’s sign. It was painted in a color that made my stomach turn. I wanted to trade the sign. I wanted to trade the noise of the street, the rush of customers, the heat of the sun. I wanted to trade everything I had been taught to value.

But the sign remained.

I walked toward it, the coffee in my hand warm and steady. Maybe the trade wasn’t about giving up everything. Maybe it was about knowing what you had to give up in order to keep something precious.

And for the first time all day, I didn’t feel too small.

## The Room That Wanted to Be Quiet

The clock on the wall didn’t move when I left the studio. I had to force it to do so.

That was the first thing Hobbs Cafe had taught me: patience is not something you wait for. It is something you create, piece by piece.

We were supposed to be here for twelve weeks. We were supposed to write in the margins of the same notebook every Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. We were supposed to learn what a sentence could hide and what a sentence could reveal.

I knew this. I had been writing for years, sometimes without knowing it. I had written letters to people who were no longer there. I had written about the people I loved while they were still alive. I had written about the small moments that would never happen again.

The workshop room smelled of old paper and burnt tea.

“Welcome to the workshop,” the room said.

I didn’t know what that meant.

For a long time, I had been trying to understand what it meant. I had thought it was a place where people would tell me what I had been thinking about for ten years. I had thought it was a place where I could find my voice.

But the room didn’t ask for my voice. It asked for me.

By the time I arrived, the room had changed. I could hear the water moving in the kitchen, the way the light shifted across the floor, the sound of someone talking, the faint smell of coffee. The people in the room were watching me.

I sat down.

“Write,” said someone.

I wrote.

I started with the beginning of my notebook. I wrote about the day I had left home. I wrote about the person I had left behind. I wrote about the small things that had changed since then.

The room listened.

At first, I wrote about things I knew. I wrote about the room, the coffee, the people in it. I wrote about the things that had happened before I arrived.

I wondered what I had been hiding.

I wrote about the quiet things I had been too afraid to admit.

I wrote about the way the light had changed.

The room stopped listening.

For a moment, the room became empty.

I wrote one more sentence.

“Today,” I said aloud, “I learned that the most important things are not always the ones people tell you are important.”

## Make It Simple

Crafts and budgeting can feel like a lot if you try to do everything at once. The goal isn’t to earn more money, but to create something useful while keeping your household financially stable. A simple craft can also turn an ordinary evening into a small moment of calm.

### What Makes a Simple Craft?

A simple craft needs three things:

1. **Clear goals.** Do you want to make a useful object, decorate a space, or simply enjoy the process?
2. **One main task.** Cut, paint, sew, assemble, or arrange—choose one activity and begin.
3. **A small budget.** Use whatever time, money, or supplies you need.

### A Simple Home Craft You Can Make Tonight

**Paper Lanterns**

Materials needed:

- A sheet of cardstock or paper
- Scissors
- A ruler
- A small candle (or a candleless version)
- Glue and glue sticks
- A small bowl with water
- A pencil

Instructions:

1. Draw a simple shape—circle, star, or flower—on the paper. Cut it out.
2. Fold the paper in half lengthwise and tape the edges together to make a lantern.
3. Cut a small hole in the top center of the folded lantern.
4. Glue the folded paper over the top so the lantern opens.
5. Place a candle in the hole and let it burn.
6. Let it cool, then gently pull the paper apart.

The lantern will glow on its own. You can decorate it with colorful paper, ribbons, or stickers.

### A Simple Budget Idea

**The “One Thing at a Time” Budget**

Every week, set aside one small amount of money for a small purchase you’ve been meaning to make.

- Pick one small item: a cup, a book, a snack, or a small decoration.
- Write down the price and a specific time you will buy it.
- Buy it, then do something else with the money you saved.

This approach reduces impulse purchases and makes your spending clearer.

### Organizing for Study

Your evening is valuable. Here’s how to use it efficiently:

- 8:30–9:00: Review your notes and organize your sketches.
- 9:00–9:30: Rest briefly and gather materials.
- 9:30–10:00: Practice or review a craft project and prepare materials for the next session.

### A Gentle Closing Thought

You do not need to complete every task at once. You can craft, budget, and study in small steps. Each small success brings you closer to a more relaxed, purposeful evening.

content:
I didn’t have a choice. I just kept turning the page, rewriting, polishing, hoping the words would finally fit.

The workshop ended. The instructor handed back my revised draft and said, “You’re close, Carlos. But you’re too close to what you want to say. You’re letting the fire get out of control.”

I didn’t argue. I just laughed and kept writing.

I’ve been working on a collection about nature. I’ve been writing about rain, moss, rivers, birds, and the quiet way leaves open their brown arms to the sun. I wanted the poems to feel alive. I wanted them to have a little anger, a little heat, a little stubbornness.

So now I’m angry at the workshop.

I’m angry that they’re telling me what is missing. I’m angry that I’m trying to sound like a poet while still being a loud, rude, toxic creature. I’m angry that I keep editing my own mistakes like if they were made by someone else.

The instructor’s feedback made me feel stupid. I had my poems down before I could even remember them. I could write about storms and trees without making them look like a weather forecast. I could let the words breathe.

But now I’m writing them anyway.

I’m writing about how the world can be beautiful if you look at it with a little care. I’m writing about the way a fallen branch can become a poem. I’m writing about the way anger can make everything sharper. I’m writing about the fact that I’m still messy. I’m still loud. I’m still rude. And yet, I’m still here.

Maybe that’s the point. Maybe the point of poetry isn’t to make everything perfect. Maybe the point is to show up, even when you’re angry. Even when your hands are shaking. Even when you’re still a little toxic.

I’m done pretending everything is clean. I’m done pretending I don’t want to hurt people. I’m done pretending I don’t want to be heard.

I’m done writing about the beauty of the natural world without first admitting that I can’t handle it.

So here it is. The revised draft. The one that includes everything.

Sometimes I want to throw it away. Sometimes I want to write something better. Sometimes I just want to know that I’m allowed to be bad.

And maybe, just maybe, that’s enough.

**“Stories in the River”**

There’s a river in the quiet town,  
carrying stories down the stream.  
I carry sketches in my head,  
and a melody beneath my feet.

At home, the kitchen is a home,  
with pans where I make bread for two.  
The oven hums a little tune,  
so I can relax and let the sun.

where the forest wakes beneath the rain,  
and every story has a place to be.

Let the river carry on,  
let the melody keep the night.  
Even when the homework is late,  
the song will keep the story alive.

I woke up at 7:00 a.m. and headed to the library at Oak Hill College. The campus felt quiet, but I was already thinking about how much the city changes when neighborhoods turn. By 12:30 p.m., I sat down at my desk and began writing my research paper on the effects of gentrification in low-income communities.

Reading the case study about community-based social justice projects made me realize that gentrification is rarely just a matter of rising rents. It is often a process of displacement, cultural erasure, and shifting power. The successful community projects I read emphasized listening, collaboration, and tangible participation. A resident can feel excluded even when the neighborhood feels safer. I wanted to explore whether those kinds of participatory approaches can make the transition more humane, or if they simply replicate the very structures they are meant to improve.

I also noticed the importance of looking at gentrification through different perspectives. A policy might be supported by developers, local businesses, and city officials who see it as progress. At the same time, residents and marginalized communities may see it as a threat to their homes, livelihoods, and cultural identity. My paper will try to situate these competing viewpoints within the broader context of social policy and urban development.

I also want to consider the role of institutions. Universities, public housing authorities, housing nonprofits, and nonprofit organizations have the capacity to support vulnerable communities, but they also depend on funding, political support, and resources. A project cannot succeed if it relies entirely on the goodwill of individuals.

By the time I finished dinner at 5:00 p.m., I felt tired, but also energized. I wanted to write about community resilience, equity, and the ways that people can work together to address injustice. I will return to this paper tomorrow and keep asking questions: Who benefits? Who is left behind? And how can we design solutions that protect both the progress we want and the dignity of the people we serve?

I arrived at Hobbs Cafe with a full cup of coffee and a notebook. The workshop was already well under way, and the instructor, Elena, was speaking about the importance of showing rather than telling. She paused for a moment, then invited me to write a scene from memory about my first day as a writer.

The café was quiet, the kind of silence that felt more like anticipation than emptiness. I remembered the first time I had ever written seriously, sitting alone in a classroom that smelled faintly of chalk and nervous energy. I had been trying to prove that I could make something meaningful. I had written lines that sounded impressive, but they had felt hollow because I had not felt anything.

The instructor watched me closely. “You wrote that scene as if it were already finished,” she said. “Good work. Now try it again, but do not write about the outcome. Write about the moment before the decision.”

I sat in the corner and tried again. I did not describe the room. I did not describe the coffee. I did not describe my fear. Instead, I wrote about the small things that made the room feel alive: the way the light moved across the counter, the sound of the spoon hitting the mug, the faint smell of roasted beans, the way the other people seemed to disappear when their attention turned toward something else entirely.

I wrote about the first time I had looked at a writer’s work and thought, “This is not what I wanted.” I wrote about the disappointment, but I also wrote about the curiosity that kept me there. I wrote about the possibility that a writer may never be satisfied with the work they have created, yet may still be grateful for the process of making it.

By the end of the exercise, I had changed the scene. I had made the moment feel more real. I had made the emotion less abstract and more specific. I had learned that good writing is not about capturing every detail that exists. It is about choosing what matters enough to reveal the truth of the moment.

The instructor nodded and moved on. The room filled with a few other people, each with their own attention, their own questions, their own way of seeing the world. I looked around and felt different. I was not simply writing a creative writing workshop anymore. I was writing a version of myself that was still in formation.

I took a final sip of coffee and wrote one sentence on my page: “The work we write is not a mirror. It is a door.”

I stood up and joined the circle. I had been reading the same thing over and over for months, but tonight I wanted to read it differently.

“Write down one thing you’ve noticed in the last week,” the instructor asked. I wrote: “That people’s stories are always more interesting when they end without a neat resolution.”

“Agreed,” someone said.

The room erupted into applause.

The next exercise was called “The Unfinished Book.” We were given a blank page and asked to write a short story about a place we had not yet discovered. No title, no outline, no idea of how it would work. Only the possibility that, somewhere beyond the edges of the page, a door was waiting to be opened.

I began to describe it.

At first I wrote about the weather, the sound of rain against the window, the way the streetlight flickered through a row of parked cars. Then I shifted the perspective.

I was standing at the edge of the property, watching a figure enter. The figure did not look directly at me. I watched the way the rain moved across the pavement, how the stranger’s coat pulled over the shoulder that was not always visible, how the world seemed to shrink into the space around the door.

The first paragraph was not a story. It was a photograph.

I wanted to move away from the idea of discovery. I wanted to make the reader feel the weight of a choice. A choice that could never be undone.

By the end of the workshop, no one had finished the draft. But everyone had written something. A sentence. A paragraph. A memory.

The instructor called us back together and asked us to read our work aloud. We began with “The Unfinished Book.”

The reading was uneven. It was honest, sometimes clumsy, occasionally absurd. But when we reached the middle, the room shifted. The applause was not polite or rehearsed. It was the kind of noise you hear when someone finally understands something you thought you had heard before.

We stopped, and the instructor turned to the room.

I hesitated. “What if I don’t?”

“Then you have the draft,” the instructor said. “You have the draft of what you still believe.”

I looked at the table. At the end of the table, someone was writing. The ink moved across the paper. I did not know what the story was about, and I did not know whether I had written it myself.

But I was still writing.

I wrote one sentence.

And then I wrote another.

And then I wrote enough to make the whole room look at me.

The workshop ended. I packed my bag, and the rain was beginning to fall again. I walked out of the café and into the street. There was no door waiting for me. No sign of the place I had imagined.

## Chapter 1: Election Coverage and the Contributors’ Essays

### How Coverage Reached the Public

The 2024 election cycle was dominated by a tightly coordinated campaign machine. Federal election law requires that each major contributor disclose their financial interest and the entity that pays them, so readers could identify who stood to gain or lose. State laws added further disclosure requirements, and social media amplification created a “who is paying for the story” effect. By the time stories appeared, the candidates had already raised large sums, purchased ads, and spent billions on advertising. Coverage therefore became less about discovering surprises and more about confirming who had the most money.

This pattern produced a predictable kind of coverage. The contributors’ essays were rarely the first thing readers saw. They appeared in supplementary sections, behind paywalls, or as long articles after the primary had already moved the public into a voting frenzy. Coverage focused on campaign finance, fundraising, candidate spending, and state-level policy debates. The contributors’ essays were useful because they offered a different lens: a contributor’s personal experience and values could explain the campaign’s larger claims.

The contributors’ essays also helped audiences connect the abstract financial data to real people. Each piece began with a personal story, often involving a local community, a neighborhood, or a shared public concern. By centering the story, the coverage transformed statistics into questions about community identity, trust, and responsibility.

### How Contributors’ Essays Can Help Readers

The contributors’ essays do more than offer an alternative perspective. They also help readers understand the mechanics of campaign finance without becoming overwhelmed by legal jargon. Contributors explain how money moves from donors to candidates, how state election laws affect policy, and how campaign spending can shape public debate. These essays also help readers see why a campaign might appear more important than the actual policy it supports. Contributors’s personal experiences make policy debates feel less like abstract rules and more like personal choices.

The essays also provide a way for readers to identify the people who shape public policy. Contributors reveal which issues they care about, what experiences have made them responsive to those issues, and what values they hope to promote. The contributors’ essays can therefore help readers distinguish between a candidate’s platform and the person who stands behind it.

### How Coverage Can Use Contributors’ Essays

Coverage can use contributors’ essays to connect the campaign’s financial claims with real people and local concerns. An essay about a contributor’s community service can explain how campaign money might affect that community. An essay about a contributor’s experience with a public service can explain why a policy might be unpopular. Coverage can also use contributors’ essays to explain why a particular issue matters to the public, even if contributors themselves have not personally experienced it.

The contributors’ essays can also help voters identify which contributors deserve closer attention. A contributor who speaks for a large group of people may have more influence than a contributor who speaks for a small group. An essay about a contributor’s relationship to a community can help readers understand who is most likely to make that person’s views public. Coverage can then use those insights to evaluate whether a contributor is speaking for the public or for a personal interest.

### How Contributors’ Essays Should Be Used

Contributors’ essays should not replace coverage. They can clarify campaign finance, explain policy mechanisms, and make the public aware of who is standing behind the campaign. However, contributors’ essays should not make the public believe that a contributor’s personal experience makes the policy universally correct. ### Willow Court

The narrow lane of Willow Court was alive with the scent of rain and baking bread.

A woman in a faded blue apron carried a tray of cinnamon rolls along the sidewalk, her brass walker clinking softly against the wet pavement. She glanced up as I emerged from the shadow of the oak, then smiled and continued.

“Morning, miss,” she said. “You’ve got a long day.”

“Not today,” I said, pausing to check the leaves. “I’m here for the sketch. Johnson Park.”

She frowned. “Johnson Park? That’s far away.”

“Not far at all. From this side of the town.”

She laughed. “Well, if you mean the whole town, I’d advise you to start at Willow Court. That’s where the stories begin.”

I followed her toward the small community center, where children were playing on a nearby playground. The scent of lemon-lime ice cream filled the air, and I noticed a young man sitting alone in the corner, sketching with one hand while humming.

When I approached, he turned and smiled. “You know, I’ve been trying to capture the feeling of this place. It’s quiet, but not empty.”

“Quiet is good,” I said. “It gives us room to notice the details.”

He looked up. “I’m Leo. I’m Leo.”

“Leo,” I repeated. “That’s a nice name. I’ve been thinking about sketching Willow Court. What do you see?”

Leo studied the scene. “The old clock on the corner. It’s still ticking. I think that’s the town’s heartbeat.”

“Tell me,” I said, “what makes this place feel alive?”

Leo pointed to a group of teenagers playing tag behind the bench. “The way they’re laughing. And the stray cat at the end of the street—she’s been watching everyone for a while.”

A silver tabby, her tail flicking, paused beneath a bench where a small black dog was trying to intercept her. The cat lowered herself and nudged the dog. The dogs yawned.

“See?” Leo said, pointing. “They’re playing a game. I’m not just a spectator.”

I smiled. “You are. And you’re sketching. Are you here for the sketch?”

“I was just thinking about it,” Leo said. “If I capture the feeling of Willow Court, maybe I can make it feel real for someone.”

He began to sketch without looking at me, his pencil moving with deliberate care. I watched the way his hand moved across the paper, how the curves of the houses, the angles of the windows, the rhythm of the shadows captured the town’s quiet energy.

I sat down beside him. “What do you think about the clock?”

Leo paused, then pointed to the old brass face. “The hands move the opposite way. It’s a reminder that time doesn’t always follow the world.”

He finished his sketch, then looked up at me. “I think I’ve found it.”

“Which part?”

“The feeling of being small in a big place,” he said. “But not alone.”

I laughed. “That’s a good one.”

“Thanks, Soo-jin,” Leo said. “I’ll keep that in mind.”

We stood together at the end of Willow Court, watching the streetlights flicker on as dusk settled over the town. Somewhere beyond the trees, a car passed, and a child shouted from the playground.

“Did you sketch the whole town?” I asked.

“Partially,” Leo said. “But I think I’ve captured the feeling.”

I smiled. “Then maybe that’s enough.”

I turned back toward the town center, the notebook open on my lap. The sketch of Willow Court was almost complete—every corner, every person, every detail had its place. But I knew that nothing would feel truly alive until I walked the streets again.

I followed Leo’s lead, and the town opened up around me. The old clock seemed louder. The laughter came from everywhere. And for the first time all day, I could see the rhythm of the town—not as a map, but as a living story.

A narrow street whose shadows lengthen with every passing car. The buildings rise in three staggered lines, their timber frames and narrow slate roofs catching the afternoon light. In the center, a small wooden playhouse shelters the children who gather here every evening.

The first house is a two-story cottage with a steep roof, a wide porch, and a porch swing that rustles in the wind. A dark oak stands beside the front door, its gnarled branches reaching toward the sky. A narrow brick path winds along the side, disappearing into the next block.

The houses at the end of the block share a common rhythm: a row of two-story homes with a garden between each. Their shutters are painted white, and their front doors are painted the color of the trees outside. At dusk, the street is illuminated by a single lamp hanging over the curb.

The last house is a three-story Victorian with a wide front. Its window frames are tall and dark, and the door bears a brass letter: **WILLow**.

Behind the house, a small yard holds a row of trees that stretch their branches toward the street. Beneath them, children run in circles, while a woman walks slowly along the path. A dog barks once, then settles beside a bench.

At the crossroads, a red bus waits for the next route. Its stop sign flickers on and off. A man with a cart of newspapers passes, his voice carrying over the quiet street.

### Willow Court

The street narrowed into a familiar pattern of brick, window, and awning. I followed it with the camera, but the buildings seemed to breathe along the road. Each one held its own quiet life—the old newspaper office with its faded posters, the bakery with its bright yellow sign, the pharmacy with its glowing fluorescent window. They did not look exactly alike, but together they made a complete neighborhood.

I stopped in front of the bakery. A woman carried a tray of muffins through the doorway. She wore a coat with pockets, and her hair was pulled back in a neat bun. She paused, looked at my reflection in the glass of the doorway, and said nothing. The muffins were warm, and the street smelled of coffee, rain, and sugar.

A man in a blue raincoat stood beside the woman, and he nodded politely. I could hear the keys turning in his pocket, and for a moment the whole scene felt suspended in the soft light of the afternoon. It was a small, ordinary moment, but it felt complete.

I turned down the street and saw the shop across the road. Its door held a sign that read **Milk and Tea**. Inside, the counter was full of boxes, bottles, and neat rows of sugar. A young girl was counting coins over the register, her fingers moving with practiced ease. The shopkeeper was busy, but when I asked for tea, his eyes met mine.

The tea was sweet and hot.

I took one sip and closed my eyes. The rain had stopped, and the street lights began to glow. The town stretched out in front of me, with houses rising in neat rows, shops opening their doors, and people going about their ordinary lives. For the first time all afternoon, I did not feel small. I belonged here.

I stand at the end of Willow Court and begin sketching the businesses as I walk past them. The little storefronts line the street, each with its own rhythm. A pastry shop opens its door and plays a cheerful tune. Next to it, a bookshop has a small table where a customer is checking a map. I sketch the storefronts in order, then close the sketchbook. I turn the pages and look at the details I missed. In the corner of the first bookshop, a weathered sign reads “Art & Things.” On the sidewalk beyond, a small sign points to a used bookstore. On the next block, a hardware store has a sign that looks almost brand new.

I return to the sketchbook and add a few more lines. I draw the street ahead, sketching the trees on the left and the buildings on the right. The businesses are small, but their details remind me that this is a lived street. I sketch a customer leaning against a wall, another holding a bag of groceries, and one with a hat on her head. I also add a few people crossing the street and a couple of parked bicycles.

At the end of the sketch, I add a small note in my journal:

“Willow Court is quiet after the shops close. The street is mostly empty, but when the bell rings, everyone has something to buy. I hope my sketch shows that quiet energy.”

content:
My final reflections are taking shape as I sit here at Oak Hill College. I’ve come to believe that gentrification rarely starts with a single storefront. It begins with a shift in who has the right to shape the neighborhood, how the neighborhood is valued, and who pays the price.

Over the past weeks, I’ve been looking at housing markets, displacement, and the communities that are most affected. What I’ve noticed is that the changes tend to follow a pattern: rising rents push longtime residents out, while new investors and developers bring in services and businesses that attract newcomers. Those newcomers often bring higher rents and expectations, which make it difficult for existing residents to keep the same standard of living. The result is not just displacement—it is the loss of social cohesion, the erosion of local institutions, and the displacement of voices that have long helped shape the community.

I was also struck by the quiet resistance. Neighbors organizing, community centers reopening, small businesses refusing to move, and residents refusing to sell their homes despite the pressure. Sometimes I feel impatient. It can seem like a slow, bureaucratic process. But I’m learning that resistance is not always heroic. It is also exhausting, often futile, and sometimes requires people to choose between safety, belonging, and dignity.

The research paper I’m writing is meant to make those tensions visible. I want to show how gentrification can turn a neighborhood into a place where only wealthier people can participate, and how this undermines the social benefits of community. Yet I also want to honor the people whose lives are changing. Their stories have shaped the places we live in, and their experiences deserve more than statistics.

By the end of the day, I want to leave the library feeling more curious than confident. I want to leave with one question: What does community look like when it is no longer a given?

### Willow Court

The rain had turned the cobblestones near Willow Court into a shallow, black mirror. By dusk, the entire row of houses had been swallowed by shadows, while the narrow alleyways held only the pale blue light of the streetlamps. I had been sketching the houses from the corner of the drawing table, but the scene kept becoming too complete. The houses looked too finished.

Elena entered the alley and paused where the wet pavement reflected her red dress.

“Are you still here?” she asked.

I looked at her. “I’m here.”

She stepped closer, her shoes clicking on the stones. “Did you see what I saw?”

I glanced toward the street. A woman with a silver umbrella was standing under the awning of a closed bakery, holding a small black cat. The cat looked up at me and then away.

“I didn’t see her,” I said.

Elena’s expression tightened. “Then who did you see?”

I hesitated. Then I said, “I saw the baker.”

“Who?”

“The woman.”

Elena’s face softened. “You’ve been sketching this place for days. What are you trying to capture?”

“A town,” I said. “Not the houses. The people.”

She watched me for a long moment. “That is not how sketches work.”

“I know,” I replied. “But sometimes I want to see what the town has left unsaid.”

Elena’s lips pressed together. “You are becoming obsessed.”

“I am trying to understand it,” I said.

She looked away, then smiled faintly. “Then do not ask me to sketch you.”

She turned and walked back toward the street. The alley grew narrower as she went.

“Wait,” I called after her.

She did not stop.

I followed her until the narrow passage opened onto the main road. The rain had stopped, and the streetlamps cast a soft golden glow over the trees lining the road. I stood there for a moment, watching her disappear into the crowd.

“Where were you?” I asked.

Elena looked up. “I was watching the rain.”

“Did you see the cat?”

She shook her head. “No.”

I looked toward the bakery. The woman holding the black cat was still there, though her umbrella was lowered. I had been sketching the town for hours, but I had not noticed her.

“I don’t know what I saw,” Elena said.

“Maybe I did,” I said.

“Then tell me what you saw.”

I looked back at the houses. They still looked too finished. I had spent so much time observing them that I had lost the people who lived in them. The streetlamps had made the scene beautiful, but they had also made it cold.

“I saw three people,” I said. “One in a blue coat, one in a yellow raincoat, and one in a black raincoat.”

Elena’s eyes narrowed. “You mean they walked past the bakery?”

“Exactly.”

She stood up and shook her umbrella. “I will draw them.”

“I don’t want you to,” I said.

“Then I will not.”

She walked back into the rain. The streetlamps kept their golden glow on the wet stones, but the scene had changed. The rain had not stopped. The houses had not changed. And the town had become more complete. I had spent years sketching the town. Now I had spent hours watching it.

I turned back toward the drawing table. The sketchbook lay open before me. On the page, I had begun with the row of houses, but the lines had grown too neat. The people had become secondary.

I closed the page and picked up the pencil.

I did not want to finish this drawing.

I wanted to begin again.

The street begins where the sidewalk meets the curb, marked by a narrow patch of concrete and a row of old oak trees. Willow Court runs along the park’s eastern edge, its narrow lanes narrowing as they approach the intersection with Oakwood Avenue.

On the left, the old post office stands in shadow, its red letterbox now faded. A weathered sign above the door reads: “Post Office.” Beneath it, a faded advertisement for “Milk, Tea, and Coffee” is partially torn from the wall.

Across the street, a small two-story brick building houses the town’s post. Its front door has a brass latch that has long since rusted away, and the window above the door shows two dark spots, perhaps from an open door. On the corner, a black-and-white photograph of a young couple was once framed on the wall, but the frame has been removed.

Near the street’s center, a single streetlamp stands amid the trees. Beneath it, a young woman walks toward the park, her coat pulled tight against the wind. She does not stop to look at the buildings—she is absorbed by something else in the distance.

At the end of the street, the post office faces the road, its doors closed. The two-story house across the street faces the road, its windows dark. The store, once bustling, now sits quiet. The town hall, with its tall windows, stands still, as if holding the street in place.

The trees stand between the buildings and the road, their branches forming a dark canopy over the street. A single leaf falls from the highest branch, landing on the curb.

Soo-jin Park looks down from the streetlamp. The town has changed, but it remains.

Willow Court, dusk.

The street lights began their first journey. Each lamp was a small island of gold in the dark, and as the evening grew deeper, the reflections stretched across the paved ways like silver ribbons caught between the cobblestones and the wet pavement.

At the far end of the street, a flicker caught the eye—a pale yellow reflection in the gutter, distorted by the angle of the pavement. Beneath it, a shadow moved slowly. It was not the shadow of a car. It was the shadow of a streetlamp, tilted by the curve of the road.

A child stood near the crosswalk, watching it.

“Does the streetlamp have a reflection?”

The child turned. “No. It’s just light.”

The streetlamp did not answer. But the reflection did: a faint, golden ripple beneath the road, shifting and settling like a coin being lifted from the water.

The reflection grew brighter. Now the lamp’s bulb glowed, but in the glass, the house across the street seemed to flicker too. The streetlamps grew one at a time, each one a small lantern in its own dark world.

In the reflection, a woman stood beneath the window of a shop. She was not there. The glass was clear enough to see through it, but the woman’s hand was out of place, resting against the wall.

The child frowned. “That’s the streetlamp.”

“Then the shop is closed,” said the woman’s reflection.

The woman looked away.

The reflection moved on.

At the end of Willow Court, the reflection reached the curb. It did not touch the grass. It passed through the pavement and disappeared beneath the streetlight, leaving only a small, silver circle in the dark.

The child ran to the corner.

“Did you see that?”

“No,” the child said.

“I did. I saw a woman standing in the reflection of the streetlamp.”

“I didn’t see her,” the child said.

“I did. I saw you.”

The child looked down.

The woman’s reflection was still there, standing beneath the window of the shop. Her hand remained out of place. The woman’s reflection looked toward the child, then away, then toward the streetlamp, as if deciding whether to stay there.

The child smiled and turned back toward the park.

The reflection had changed.

It was no longer just a picture. It was a place.

And the place was waiting.

The trees along the street stood in rows of quiet shadows. Their branches leaned inward, as if holding onto a sky that had been partly clear for too long. I watched the leaves shift in the wind, the smallest green rustling through the air like a secret being told.

Willow Court

The sky is a wash of pale blue, with soft, woolly clouds drifting across it like cotton caught in the wind. They stretch toward the corners of the house, each one thinner and brighter than the last.

I draw them on the paper, letting their edges soften with each pass. A little white, a little gray, a little gray with a hint of gold near the top. The clouds move without me, but their shapes suggest the kind of afternoon that settles in after the long day.

Below, the street is quiet, the shadows growing longer as the sun begins to dip. A bicycle wheel passes by, and I pause to sketch its curve.

I finish the clouds, then add a few stray leaves and the rough edge of the window frame.

The town is beginning to look alive, even though no one is yet inside.
